The choice also changes the comparison group. Under the pooled reference period every untreated observation serves as a control. That includes never-treated cohorts, cohorts treated after the end of the sample, and the pre-treatment periods of cohorts not yet treated, apart from any pre-treatment horizons the run asks for. Parallel trends and no anticipation must then hold across all of those periods. Under *esfixedbaseperiod* each treated cohort's pre-treatment periods other than the reference period carry their own indicators, and the reference period only anchors that cohort's own level. Under *timetrends* the period immediately before the reference period also carries no indicator, and the two together anchor the cohort's level and trend. The period effects then come from never-treated cohorts and cohorts treated after the end of the sample alone. Cohorts not yet treated do not serve as controls. Parallel trends is needed only between each treated cohort and those cohorts, from the reference period on. This is the never-treated comparison of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) and Sun and Abraham (2021). The pooled default instead matches the imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess (2023) under the conditions given in chapter 15.

verdict.reason: The guide sentence claims to restate the 2026-09-07 ruling but changes its substance. The ruling says randomization inference assumes exchangeability in assignment and fails when treated clusters are heterogeneous in variance. The guide says instead that it fails when onset is related to the outcome path, and that this is the identifying assumption the design already needs. That drops the MacKinnon-Webb failure mode, which is the one that matters in the few-treated-cluster case the bootstrap refers to permute() for. It also implies that believing parallel trends is enough for valid randomization inference. Exchangeable assignment is strictly stronger than parallel trends: random timing implies parallel trends but not the reverse (Roth and Sant'Anna 2023). And RI with the coefficient statistic is mis-sized under heterogeneous treated-cluster variance even when parallel trends holds. The guide's own chapter 6 and the runtime caution both say this, so the chapter 5 sentence contradicts them. No author ruling endorses the guide's wording. The wording seems to echo the ado comment above the permute() exchangeability caution, which calls assignment exchangeability 'the design assumption'. But that comment is not a ruling, and the caution printed on the very next line states the variance failure mode. Kind and severity are about right: medium, because it misleads in exactly the use case where it matters.

verdict.reason: The finding holds, but its severity should be low. wooldid_permstep (wooldid.ado, near line 18280) builds every step from one set of permutation draws, all generated under the global sharp null. Each horizon is studentized by the SD of all its draws, and step j takes the max over the not-yet-rejected horizons in that same draw matrix. Nothing re-randomizes under a partial null. Now suppose some horizons have an effect and others have none. A reassigned onset moves the real effect into other horizons' draws. The docs describe this same mechanism for pre-treatment statistics. So the intersection nulls do not satisfy the randomization hypothesis, subset pivotality fails, and only weak FWER control is established (Westfall and Young 1993; Romano and Wolf 2005). The package's own evidence covers only the global null. F058 s5.4/s6.5 measured step-down FWER under D1, tau = 0 on every horizon. permute_coverage_2026-09-02 s3.1 argues the step-down is valid only because 'the joint null is the sharp null', which is the weak-control argument. There is no author ruling on strong versus weak control. rulings_2026-09-07 s.G rules only on the default (opt-in), the scope (pre as a separate family) and the engine (permutation only). An unqualified 'controls the family-wise error rate' reads as strong control, and strong control is the only thing a step-down adds over the single-step max. So the help sentence overclaims. Severity is low rather than medium: sd comes from the contaminated draws, which shrinks t_obs, and the |draws| are wider and off-centre, which raises the max. Both push truly null horizons toward non-rejection, so the likely practical cost is lost power, not excess size. That direction is not proven, though, so the docs should say 'not guaranteed' rather than 'conservative'. My fix improves on the reviewer's in three ways. (1) It drops 'of the family' from the exactness clause. Effects at horizons outside the family (post effects for the pre family, anticipation for the post family) contaminate the draws too, and the guide already says the pre family is conservative because of post effects. The accurate null is the docs' own phrase elsewhere: 'the sharp null of no effect at any horizon'. (2) It rewrites the next guide sentence, which says the pre family is conservative 'in a way the post-treatment family's are not'. With the new text that contrast becomes false for a post family with mixed effects. The same sentence also points to the pre-treatment caveat 'below', but that caveat is in 'What the test assumes', above this paragraph. (3) It keeps the help to one qualifying clause, since the help is being pared down, and puts the mechanism in the guide.

threatening identification. Specify *safety(off)* before the run to proceed anyway, which downgrades the refusal to a caution.

**What the ame Measures:** Within a treated cell, the ame compares units that received different doses. The choice of g() sets the parallel trends assumption: without treatment, units at different doses would have followed the same outcome path, apart from the dose effects g() allows for. Under that assumption the att is identified, and so is the att within each bin of the continuous treatment effects plots. The ame is the effect of a marginal increase in the dose only under a stronger condition: units at different doses would also have gained the same from treatment at any given dose. This is the strong parallel trends assumption of Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024, 'Difference-in-Differences with a Continuous Treatment', NBER Working Paper 32117). Without it, the ame also carries selection bias, since the units that took higher doses may simply be the units that gain more from treatment. The same applies to the ame within each bin and to differences in att across the bins of the continuous treatment effects plots. Under *contreatwithin* with no untreated group, the att is essentially the integral of the ame, so it needs the same stronger condition.

verdict.reason: The finding holds up. The help and the guide call the ame 'the average marginal effect of the continuous treatment'. They say g() sets 'the reference effect' and that byTime is 'analogous to the second diff'. Neither document says what makes a slope across doses causal. Here is the econometrics. g() absorbs the untreated dose slope for each group, and byTime adds one for each period. The treated cell's dose slope net of that reference slope is then d/dd of E[dY|D=d] in the cell. Under parallel trends across doses, in the form g() models, this equals dATT(d|d)/dd. Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024) show that this equals ACRT(d|d) plus a selection-bias term dATT(d|l)/dl at l=d. That term is zero under strong parallel trends, or equivalently no selection on gains. Ordinary parallel trends identifies att at the units' own doses and att within each cfx bin. It does not identify the ame, or differences in att across bins, as a causal response. The same holds for att under contreatwithin. With no untreated group, the help says that att 'should essentially be the integral of the estimated average marginal effects', so it is built from comparisons across doses and needs the same stronger condition. 'A bit speculative' is a hedge, not a condition. No author ruling covers this (see evidence). The kind label DOC_ECONOMETRIC_ERROR is acceptable, but the defect is an omitted identifying condition, not a false statement. Severity medium stands, because the ame is a headline output and users will read it as the effect of a larger dose. The reviewer's text needed two changes. First, the parallel trends it states must be the g()-relative version ('apart from the dose effects g() allows for'), not identical untreated paths across doses, since basic, byCohort and byTime all allow baseline dose slopes. Second, contreatwithin should be named. The citation list also lacks the paper, so an entry is added.

verdict.reason: The finding holds. Without bootstrap(), the analytic band is built from e(V_es_<family>) with no cluster gate. wooldid_esband's analytic branch reads that matrix unconditionally, and wooldid_esbanda sets the band to b +/- c*sqrt(diag V), taking c from the correlation matrix implied by V. The band is therefore scaled by the event-study analytic standard errors. The help's clustering discussion and guide list item 2 say those standard errors are understated without a caution when cluster() is at or above i: the saturated cell dummies zero out each treated cell's cluster score. So the band is too narrow in exactly that design, and nothing cautions. The guide's own table is internally inconsistent here. The jointtests and pretrendpower rows list 'analytic cluster() at or above i', and guide 1370 says pretrendpower 'reads the same covariance'. The band reads it too, yet its row says 'none'. This is not RULED. The nearest ruling is changes_review_2026-09-22.md l.261, 'band covers 0.90 at 10 clusters (measurement) | Leave the docs'. It answered round-2 item esband-tlaw-undercover-10clus, which concerned a different mechanism: 10 clusters below i, df_r 9, where the pointwise intervals still covered 0.95 and only the sup-t simulation fell short. The t-law and no-floor rulings (l.49, l.73) concern the critical value's law and are untouched. The author has not ruled on the band under cluster at or above i. He should see the adjacency to l.261 and may extend that ruling if he wants. Two corrections to the reviewer's proposal. The paragraph itself shows that sentence 1 does not mean differential trends: a few sentences later it names 'cohorts not being on the same outcome trends' as a separate ingredient. That leaves the common-trend reading, which is wrong. I first considered a rescue reading: unit-level persistent, random-walk-like outcomes, under which the pooled reference loses its precision edge (BJS 2024 versus Harmon 2022). But the words do not say serial correlation, and the guide shows how the sentence gets read. Guide:417 turns the hedge into a flat directive: 'Prefer the fixed reference when the outcome trends within the pre-period'. That sends any user with a secularly trending outcome, such as log wages, away from the more precise default for no gain. The reviewer's direction checks algebraically. Take a linear differential pre-trend d with K pooled pre-periods. At horizon h, the fixed -1 reference has bias (h+1)d and the pooled reference has bias (h+(K+1)/2)d, so the pooled reference is worse whenever K>1. There is no ruling: nothing in review_process/ mentions 'evolving over time' or 'trends within the pre'.

verdict.reason: The reviewer calls this 'the same mechanism as F4', but it is not. In F4, the triple difference, the two group-level DiDs share a cohort-by-period shock, and the contrast exists to cancel it. When the groups weight their cells differently, a bias term sum (w1-w0) s_ct survives, so 'will be the triple diff estimate' was wrong. Here each arm's ATT is identified on its own against the clean comparison group. It is a convex, nonnegatively weighted average of that arm's cell effects. No shared shock is left that the contrast is meant to remove. The arm contrast is the difference of two well-defined estimands. Arms can differ in onset timing or exposure, but that is the generic caveat of every aggregate across horizons and composition. The help already covers it at sthlp:991 (the sumstat composition note), with the per-subgroup event-study rows, and in the subgroups section (within-cell subgroup variation, with the remedy i = group(i sg)). The sentence is also an overview and is hedged ('This can be useful for'). The de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille negative-weights concern does not apply, because wooldid's subgroup weights are nonnegative cell shares. No author ruling was needed or found.
verdict.evidence: sthlp:150-154 (overview paragraph): 'This can be useful for tests of differences in treatment efficacy across treatment arms and can be used to replicate functionality that interaction terms in a traditional difference-in-differences would have provided.' Subgroups section (sthlp ~660-668) already warns that where the subgroup varies within a cell the contrasts only reweight pooled cell effects, with remedy egen newi = group(i sg). F4 verdict (lookup.json ident:F4) rests on the shared-shock term s_ct, which has no counterpart in an arm-vs-arm ATT contrast.

verdict.reason: The theory the finding cites is correct. Ibragimov and Muller (2010) Theorem 1, from Bakirov and Szekely (2006), guarantees the t(q-1) test is conservative under heterogeneous cluster variances only for alpha <= 2*Phi(-sqrt 3) = 0.0833. But the docs make no false statement: they only describe the reference distribution. The uncovered range is also numerically immaterial. I simulated the worst case directly: the supremum over variance configurations is attained with k equal nonzero variances among q, and I searched over k. At alpha = 0.10 (level(90)) the worst size was 0.1000 at q=20, 0.1005 at q=50 and 0.1010 at q=200. The q to infinity limit peaks at about 0.1011 (k around 10-15). MC standard errors were about 0.0002. So at level(90) the over-rejection is at most about 0.1 percentage point. That is well below any application's own noise, and it is dwarfed by the independence and shared-control-pool caveats the help and guide already carry for impvalues. Adding the 8.3 percent sentence would make the reader worry about a 10.1 percent versus 10 percent issue. grep of review_process/ found no ruling, and none is needed.

verdict.reason: The algebra holds. Scale the Dirichlet(1,...,1) weights by G: each has mean 1, variance (G-1)/(G+1) and covariance -1/(G+1). The multinomial pairs-bootstrap counts have mean 1, variance (G-1)/G and covariance -1/G. The two covariance matrices are c(I - J/G) with c = G/(G+1) and c = 1, so they differ by exactly the factor G/(G+1) (Rubin 1981). The first moments are shared and the second are not. That makes 'whose first two moments it shares' false at finite G: the variance factor is 0.91 at G=10. The project's own blue-sky agent computed the same G/(G+1) and flagged the phrase (mc-boot-perm-size NOTES 239-241). It also measured larger gaps on real designs (SD ratio 0.81 at G=10, and 0.64 with one dominant weight), so the phrase undersells the difference. The wording entered with commit 9bcb462 (F050). verdict.reason: The author approved this exact clause word for word when he ruled that the permute() equality tests and pairwise contrasts be labelled as sharp-null tests. The footer text, including 'so a common nonzero effect alone can reject them', is in changes_review_2026-09-22.md:68 and was built in 66d6680. Guide 383 paraphrases that approved footer (ado:13197). The clause is also defensible, so the finding's 'not correct' goes too far. Under permute(shuffle) without permstrata(), the shuffle also re-randomizes which subgroups the treated clusters fall in. A common effect then pushes each subgroup's permuted estimate off zero by an amount that depends on the subgroup's treated share, so the contrast's null can sit off centre while the observed contrast is near zero. The engine flags exactly that case (e(perm_offcentre)). The reviewer's probe used only permstrata(sg), where the null stays centred and widens, so the test loses power. The two behaviours are design-dependent, and 'can reject' is a claim that it is possible, not a statement of which way it always goes. One caveat on the supporting evidence: the audit's D4 case (common effect, no strata, pairwise p=.0103 with the contrast flagged off centre) is suggestive, not clean. The analytic equality p on those data was 8.3e-6, and the permutation equality p was 1.000, which is the reviewer's direction. The fair reading is that both directions occur. Adding the power-loss half is a wording refinement, and because it touches an approved runtime message it needs the author's clearance.

verdict.reason: The code facts are right, but the claimed econometric error is not. In wooldid_advW, alt == 0 whitens on the eigenvectors with lam > 1e-12*max|lam|, drops b's null-space component and sets q = rank(V) - rank(M). That is the standard generalized-inverse Wald statistic (Moore 1977; Andrews 1987), and it is the same convention Stata's own -test- follows when it drops constraints and reports reduced df. When V is the true covariance, b - beta lies in col(V) under H0, so the retained statistic is correctly sized. The dropped directions cost power only. They do not bias the p-value, so 'biases it toward non-rejection' overstates the effect. Where the rank deficiency is an artefact of the estimated V (few clusters, singleton cells), the help already says the analytic test is severely oversized and names permute()/bootstrap(). The documents do not misdescribe the behaviour. The guide's adversarial entry says the line is fit 'by generalized least squares under a generalized inverse of that covariance' with numerator df equal to 'the rank of the event-study covariance minus one'. It also says 'A p-value is produced whenever the covariance has positive rank'. So 'degenerate' in the help and guide means no positive rank, not rank-deficient, and the help's 'cancelled ... when the event-study covariance is degenerate' is true. The wooldid_advstat comment lists every way the p can fail across both branches. The column-space item belongs to alt == 1, so the comment is imprecise but not false. What remains is the lack of a run-time signal that the truncation fired. That is a disclosure gap already on file as blue-sky finding hv-adv-ame-rank (CONFIRMED, 'disclosure-only'), whose refuter judged the eigen-truncation 'the statistically correct treatment of a structurally non-identified direction'. I found no author ruling on it in RULINGS_LEDGER.md, fix_proposal_status.md, changes_review_2026-09-22.md or held_for_ruling_*.md.

new_verdicts.reason: The guide sentence claims to restate the 2026-09-07 ruling but changes its substance. The ruling says randomization inference assumes exchangeability in assignment and fails when treated clusters are heterogeneous in variance. The guide says instead that it fails when onset is related to the outcome path, and that this is the identifying assumption the design already needs. That drops the MacKinnon-Webb failure mode, which is the one that matters in the few-treated-cluster case the bootstrap refers to permute() for. It also implies that believing parallel trends is enough for valid randomization inference. Exchangeable assignment is strictly stronger than parallel trends: random timing implies parallel trends but not the reverse (Roth and Sant'Anna 2023). And RI with the coefficient statistic is mis-sized under heterogeneous treated-cluster variance even when parallel trends holds. The guide's own chapter 6 and the runtime caution both say this, so the chapter 5 sentence contradicts them. No author ruling endorses the guide's wording. The wording seems to echo the ado comment above the permute() exchangeability caution, which calls assignment exchangeability 'the design assumption'. Kind and severity are about right: medium, because it misleads in exactly the use case where it matters.

new_verdicts.reason: The finding holds, but its severity should be low. wooldid_permstep (wooldid.ado, near line 18280) builds every step from one set of permutation draws, all generated under the global sharp null. Each horizon is studentized by the SD of all its draws, and step j takes the max over the not-yet-rejected horizons in that same draw matrix. Nothing re-randomizes under a partial null. Now suppose some horizons have an effect and others have none. A reassigned onset moves the real effect into other horizons' draws. The docs describe this same mechanism for pre-treatment statistics. So the intersection nulls do not satisfy the randomization hypothesis, subset pivotality fails, and only weak FWER control is established (Westfall and Young 1993; Romano and Wolf 2005). The package's own evidence covers only the global null. F058 s5.4/s6.5 measured step-down FWER under D1, tau = 0 on every horizon. permute_coverage_2026-09-02 s3.1 argues the step-down is valid only because 'the joint null is the sharp null', which is the weak-control argument. There is no author ruling on strong versus weak control. rulings_2026-09-07 s.G rules only on the default (opt-in), the scope (pre as a separate family) and the engine (permutation only). An unqualified 'controls the family-wise error rate' reads as strong control, and strong control is the only thing a step-down adds over the single-step max. So the help sentence overclaims. Severity is low rather than medium: sd comes from the contaminated draws, which shrinks t_obs, and the |draws| are wider and off-centre, which raises the max. Both push truly null horizons toward non-rejection, so the likely practical cost is lost power, not excess size. That direction is not proven, though, so the docs should say 'not guaranteed' rather than 'conservative'. My fix improves on the reviewer's in three ways. (1) It drops 'of the family' from the exactness clause. Effects at horizons outside the family (post effects for the pre family, anticipation for the post family) contaminate the draws too, and the guide already says the pre family is conservative because of post effects. The accurate null is the docs' own phrase elsewhere: 'the sharp null of no effect at any horizon'. (2) It rewrites the next guide sentence, which says the pre family is conservative 'in a way the post-treatment family's are not'. With the new text that contrast becomes false for a post family with mixed effects. The same sentence also points to the pre-treatment caveat 'below', but that caveat is in 'What the test assumes', above this paragraph. (3) It keeps the help to one qualifying clause, since the help is being pared down, and puts the mechanism in the guide.

new_verdicts.reason: The guide says without condition that when the treated clusters are atypical, the reference distribution is narrower than the observed statistic's sampling distribution. MacKinnon and Webb (2020) find that this failure runs both ways for the coefficient-based randomization test. It over-rejects when the treated clusters are small and under-rejects when they are large. So the guide's sentence is wrong whenever the treated clusters are larger or quieter than the controls: the reference distribution is then the wider one, and the p-value is too large, not too small. No author ruling covers the direction. rulings_2026-09-07.md lines 209-211 say only that randomization inference 'fails when treated clusters are heterogeneous in variance'. That matches either direction, so it is not a ruling that only one direction applies. The finding stands. I judge the severity as low rather than medium. The direction the guide does state is the dangerous, anti-conservative one, and it is stated correctly. The error misdescribes only the conservative case, where a reader loses power, not test size.

new_verdicts.reason: The finding holds up. The help and the guide call the ame 'the average marginal effect of the continuous treatment'. They say g() sets 'the reference effect' and that byTime is 'analogous to the second diff'. Neither document says what makes a slope across doses causal. Here is the econometrics. g() absorbs the untreated dose slope for each group, and byTime adds one for each period. The treated cell's dose slope net of that reference slope is then d/dd of E[dY|D=d] in the cell. Under parallel trends across doses, in the form g() models, this equals dATT(d|d)/dd. Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024) show that this equals ACRT(d|d) plus a selection-bias term dATT(d|l)/dl at l=d. That term is zero under strong parallel trends, or equivalently no selection on gains. Ordinary parallel trends identifies att at the units' own doses and att within each cfx bin. It does not identify the ame, or differences in att across bins, as a causal response. The same holds for att under contreatwithin. With no untreated group, the help says that att 'should essentially be the integral of the estimated average marginal effects', so it is built from comparisons across doses and needs the same stronger condition. 'A bit speculative' is a hedge, not a condition. No author ruling covers this (see evidence). The kind label DOC_ECONOMETRIC_ERROR is acceptable, but the defect is an omitted identifying condition, not a false statement. Severity medium stands, because the ame is a headline output and users will read it as the effect of a larger dose. The reviewer's text needed two changes. First, the parallel trends it states must be the g()-relative version ('apart from the dose effects g() allows for'), not identical untreated paths across doses, since basic, byCohort and byTime all allow baseline dose slopes. Second, contreatwithin should be named. The citation list also lacks the paper, so an entry is added.

Help:622-623 (the author's original prose, fc17051) says the pooled reference is 'likely disadvantageous whenever the outcome variable is evolving over time within the pre-treatment period'. Read plainly, that means the outcome trends. A trend common to treated and comparison cohorts is absorbed by the period effects and costs the pooled reference nothing. The paragraph itself shows that sentence 1 does not mean differential trends: a few sentences later it names 'cohorts not being on the same outcome trends' as a separate ingredient. That leaves the common-trend reading, which is wrong. I first considered a rescue reading: unit-level persistent, random-walk-like outcomes, under which the pooled reference loses its precision edge (BJS 2024 versus Harmon 2022). But the words do not say serial correlation, and the guide shows how the sentence gets read. Guide:417 turns the hedge into a flat directive: 'Prefer the fixed reference when the outcome trends within the pre-period'. That sends any user with a secularly trending outcome, such as log wages, away from the more precise default for no gain. The reviewer's direction checks algebraically. Take a linear differential pre-trend d with K pooled pre-periods. At horizon h, the fixed -1 reference has bias (h+1)d and the pooled reference has bias (h+(K+1)/2)d, so the pooled reference is worse whenever K>1. There is no ruling: nothing in review_process/ mentions 'evolving over time' or 'trends within the pre'.

new_verdicts.reason: The reviewer calls this 'the same mechanism as F4', but it is not. In F4, the triple difference, the two group-level DiDs share a cohort-by-period shock, and the contrast exists to cancel it. When the groups weight their cells differently, a bias term sum (w1-w0) s_ct survives, so 'will be the triple diff estimate' was wrong. Here each arm's ATT is identified on its own against the clean comparison group. It is a convex, nonnegatively weighted average of that arm's cell effects. No shared shock is left that the contrast is meant to remove. The arm contrast is the difference of two well-defined estimands. Arms can differ in onset timing or exposure, but that is the generic caveat of every aggregate across horizons and composition. The help already covers it at sthlp:991 (the sumstat composition note), with the per-subgroup event-study rows, and in the subgroups section (within-cell subgroup variation, with the remedy i = group(i sg)). The sentence is also an overview and is hedged ('This can be useful for'). The de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille negative-weights concern does not apply, because wooldid's subgroup weights are nonnegative cell shares. No author ruling was needed or found.

new_verdicts.reason: The theory the finding cites is correct. Ibragimov and Muller (2010) Theorem 1, from Bakirov and Szekely (2006), guarantees the t(q-1) test is conservative under heterogeneous cluster variances only for alpha <= 2*Phi(-sqrt 3) = 0.0833. But the docs make no false statement: they only describe the reference distribution. The uncovered range is also numerically immaterial. I simulated the worst case directly: the supremum over variance configurations is attained with k equal nonzero variances among q, and I searched over k. At alpha = 0.10 (level(90)) the worst size was 0.1000 at q=20, 0.1005 at q=50 and 0.1010 at q=200. The q to infinity limit peaks at about 0.1011 (k around 10-15). MC standard errors were about 0.0002. So at level(90) the over-rejection is at most about 0.1 percentage point. That is well below any application's own noise, and it is dwarfed by the independence and shared-control-pool caveats the help and guide already carry for impvalues. Adding the 8.3 percent sentence would make the reader worry about a 10.1 percent versus 10 percent issue. grep of review_process/ found no ruling, and none is needed.

new_verdicts.reason: The algebra holds. Scale the Dirichlet(1,...,1) weights by G: each has mean 1, variance (G-1)/(G+1) and covariance -1/(G+1). The multinomial pairs-bootstrap counts have mean 1, variance (G-1)/G and covariance -1/G. The two covariance matrices are c(I - J/G) with c = G/(G+1) and c = 1, so they differ by exactly the factor G/(G+1) (Rubin 1981). The first moments are shared and the second are not. That makes 'whose first two moments it shares' false at finite G: the variance factor is 0.91 at G=10. The project's own blue-sky agent computed the same G/(G+1) and flagged the phrase (mc-boot-perm-size NOTES 239-241). It also measured larger gaps on real designs (SD ratio 0.81 at G=10, and 0.64 with one dominant weight), so the phrase undersells the difference. The wording entered with commit 9bcb462 (F050). The F050 ruling covers the fewer-than-6-treated trigger, not this clause, and no ruling on the clause's accuracy exists in review_process/. The caution wording is a runtime message. Under the standing new-message check-in rule and the message-review artifact it needs the author's clearance, and two tests pin the exact string.

new_verdicts.reason: The author approved this exact clause word for word when he ruled that the permute() equality tests and pairwise contrasts be labelled as sharp-null tests. The footer text, including 'so a common nonzero effect alone can reject them', is in changes_review_2026-09-22.md:68 and was built in 66d6680. Guide 383 paraphrases that approved footer (ado:13197). The clause is also defensible, so the finding's 'not correct' goes too far. Under permute(shuffle) without permstrata(), the shuffle also re-randomizes which subgroups the treated clusters fall in. A common effect then pushes each subgroup's permuted estimate off zero by an amount that depends on the subgroup's treated share, so the contrast's null can sit off centre while the observed contrast is near zero. The engine flags exactly that case (e(perm_offcentre)). The reviewer's probe used only permstrata(sg), where the null stays centred and widens, so the test loses power. The two behaviours are design-dependent, and 'can reject' is a claim that it is possible, not a statement of which way it always goes. One caveat on the supporting evidence: the audit's D4 case (common effect, no strata, pairwise p=.0103 with the contrast flagged off centre) is suggestive, not clean. The analytic equality p on those data was 8.3e-6, and the permutation equality p was 1.000, which is the reviewer's direction. The fair reading is that both directions occur. Adding the power-loss half is a wording refinement, and because it touches an approved runtime message it needs the author's clearance.

new_verdicts.reason: The code facts are right, but the claimed econometric error is not. In wooldid_advW, alt == 0 whitens on the eigenvectors with lam > 1e-12*max|lam|, drops b's null-space component and sets q = rank(V) - rank(M). That is the standard generalized-inverse Wald statistic (Moore 1977; Andrews 1987), and it is the same convention Stata's own -test- follows when it drops constraints and reports reduced df. When V is the true covariance, b - beta lies in col(V) under H0, so the retained statistic is correctly sized. The dropped directions cost power only. They do not bias the p-value, so 'biases it toward non-rejection' overstates the effect. Where the rank deficiency is an artefact of the estimated V (few clusters, singleton cells), the help already says the analytic test is severely oversized and names permute()/bootstrap(). The documents do not misdescribe the behaviour. The guide's adversarial entry says the line is fit 'by generalized least squares under a generalized inverse of that covariance' with numerator df equal to 'the rank of the event-study covariance minus one'. It also says 'A p-value is produced whenever the covariance has positive rank'. So 'degenerate' in the help and guide means no positive rank, not rank-deficient, and the help's 'cancelled ... when the event-study covariance is degenerate' is true. The wooldid_advstat comment lists every way the p can fail across both branches. The column-space item belongs to alt == 1, so the comment is imprecise but not false. What remains is the lack of a run-time signal that the truncation fired. That is a disclosure gap already on file as blue-sky finding hv-adv-ame-rank (CONFIRMED, 'disclosure-only'), whose refuter judged the eigen-truncation 'the statistically correct treatment of a structurally non-identified direction'. I found no author ruling on it in RULINGS_LEDGER.md, fix_proposal_status.md, changes_review_2026-09-22.md or held_for_ruling_*.md.

verdict.reason: The finding holds on independent reading, and no author ruling covers it. On the default poisson path wooldid passes no vce() to ppmlhdfe (vcespecifier is empty unless robust or cluster() is typed), and ppmlhdfe turns an unadjusted request into a robust one (ppmlhdfe.ado:216, 'PPML uses robust SEs'). So the variance behind every gteffects cell is heteroskedasticity-robust. With a unit-level i each treated cell is one row. The cell dummy's Poisson first-order condition sets that row's residual to zero, so the sandwich meat gets nothing from the cell. This is the same zero-residual blind spot the observation branch already reports under robust (Chesher and Jewitt 1987). But the observation branch of the containment screen only checks robust, pweight, hc2/hc3 and a robust customvce(). It has no poisson arm. A default poisson run therefore prints no caution and posts no e(gt_ncontained), and its numbers match the robust run that does get disclosed. The help at :907 is accurate about when the caution fires but implies the understatement is always reported, which is false on this path. The package makes the same mistake in three places: the screen, the wdr4alt remedy list in the vzero caution, and e(vce)=oim. That looks like one oversight, not a convention the author chose. Kind CODE_ECONOMETRIC_ERROR and severity medium stand as filed. It is the same class of silent gap that the GTE-4 reviews required closing for customvce(robust) and hc2.
